## EFT Error Investigation and Resolution (12 CFR 1005.11)

**Qualifying notice.** The institution must follow error-resolution procedures for any oral or written notice of error received no later than 60 days after it sends the periodic statement first reflecting the alleged error, provided the notice identifies the consumer's name/account number and indicates why an error is believed to exist (12 CFR 1005.11(b)(1)). The institution may require written confirmation of an oral notice within 10 business days (1005.11(b)(2)).

**Standard 10-business-day period (1005.11(c)(1)).** Investigate promptly and determine whether an error occurred within 10 business days of receiving the notice; report results to the consumer within 3 business days after completing the investigation; and correct any error within 1 business day after determining it occurred.

**45-day extension (1005.11(c)(2)).** If it cannot finish within 10 business days, the institution may take up to 45 days provided it: (i) provisionally credits the account for the alleged error amount (plus interest where applicable) within 10 business days — though it may withhold a MAXIMUM of $50 if it has a reasonable basis to believe an unauthorized EFT occurred and has satisfied § 1005.6(a); (ii) advises the consumer of the provisional credit within 2 business days and gives full use of the funds; (iii) corrects any error within 1 business day of determination; and (iv) reports results within 3 business days of completing the investigation. Provisional credit is NOT required if the institution requires but does not receive written confirmation of an oral notice within 10 business days, or the account is subject to Regulation T.

**Time extensions (1005.11(c)(3)).** 20 business days apply in place of 10 if the notice involves a transfer within 30 days after the first deposit to the account. 90 days apply in place of 45 for completing the investigation if the error involves a transfer that was not initiated within a state, resulted from a point-of-sale debit card transaction, or occurred within 30 days after the first deposit.

**Investigation scope (1005.11(c)(4)).** Except for transfers covered by § 1005.14, review of the institution's own records suffices if the alleged error concerns a transfer to/from a third party and there is no agreement with that third party for the EFT type involved.

**No error / different error (1005.11(d)).** The institution must provide a written explanation of its findings and note the consumer's right to request the documents relied upon (providing copies promptly on request). If it debits a previously provisional credit, it must (1) notify the consumer of the date and amount of the debit, and (2) honor checks/drafts/preauthorized transfers (without overdraft charge) for 5 business days after notification, to the extent it would have paid them had the credit not been debited.

## Liability Limits for Lost or Stolen Access Devices

When an access device is lost or stolen and unauthorized electronic fund transfers occur, the consumer's liability depends on when the consumer notifies the financial institution. The framework is tiered.

### Threshold Conditions (12 CFR 1005.6(a))
A consumer may be held liable only if the financial institution has:
- Provided the disclosures required by § 1005.7(b)(1), (2), and (3);
- Issued an accepted access device; and
- Provided a means to identify the consumer to whom it was issued.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0697_chunk_0001]

### Tier 1 — Notice Within Two Business Days (1005.6(b)(1))
Maximum liability = lesser of $50 OR the total amount of unauthorized transfers occurring before notice.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001]

### Tier 2 — Notice After Two Business Days, Up to 60 Calendar Days (1005.6(b)(2))
Maximum liability = lesser of $500 OR the sum of: (a) $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers in the first two business days, whichever is less; AND (b) the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring after the close of two business days and before notice — provided the institution establishes those transfers would not have occurred had the consumer notified it within the two-day period.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001]

### Tier 3 — Notice More Than 60 Calendar Days After Statement Transmittal (1005.6(b)(3))
- For transfers occurring within the 60-day period: the lesser of $500, OR the sum of (a) the lesser of $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers in the first two business days, AND (b) the amount of unauthorized transfers occurring after two business days.
- For transfers occurring after the 60-day period: unlimited liability until the financial institution is notified — provided the institution establishes those transfers would not have occurred had the consumer notified it within the 60-day period.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001] [C:exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0698_chunk_0001]

### Extension of Time Limits (1005.6(b)(4))
If the consumer's delay in notifying was due to extenuating circumstances, the institution must extend the applicable time periods to a reasonable period.
[C:12CFR1005_1005.6_chunk_0001]

### Limitations on Imposing Liability
- A financial institution may impose less liability than Regulation E permits, based on state law or the deposit agreement (1005.6(b)(6)).
- Liability is determined solely by the consumer's promptness in notifying the institution; consumer negligence, a deposit agreement, or state law may not be used to impose greater liability than Regulation E allows.

Initial Disclosures for Electronic Fund Transfer Services (12 CFR 1005.7)

Timing (1005.7(a)): A financial institution must make the required disclosures at the time the consumer contracts for an EFT service or before the first EFT is made involving the consumer's account.

Required content (1005.7(b)), as applicable:
1. Liability of consumer – a summary of the consumer's liability under § 1005.6 or under state/other applicable law or agreement for unauthorized EFTs. Need not be given if the institution imposes no liability, but must be given before imposing any liability (Comment 1005.7(b)(1)-1).
2. Telephone number and address – of the person/office to be notified when the consumer believes an unauthorized EFT has been or may be made (a specific number/address for reporting a lost/stolen access device or possible unauthorized transfer must be provided on or with the statement).
3. Business days – the institution's business days.
4. Types of transfers; limitations – the types of EFTs the consumer may make and any limitations on frequency and dollar amount; details may be withheld where confidentiality is essential to system security (but the existence of limitations must still be disclosed).
5. Fees – any fees imposed for EFTs or for the right to make transfers.
6. Documentation – a summary of the consumer's right to receipts and periodic statements under § 1005.9 and notices regarding preauthorized transfers under § 1005.10(a) and (d).
7. Stop payment – a summary of the right to stop payment of a preauthorized EFT and the procedure to do so under § 1005.10(c).
8. Liability of institution – a summary of the institution's liability under section 910 of the Act for failure to make or stop certain transfers.
9. Confidentiality – the circumstances under which the institution may, in the ordinary course of business, provide account information to third parties.
10. Error resolution – a notice substantially similar to Model Form A-3 (Appendix A) concerning error resolution.
11. ATM fees – a notice that a fee may be imposed by an ATM operator (§ 1005.16(a)) and by any network used to complete the transaction.

Addition of new EFT services (1005.7(c)): If an EFT service is added with terms and conditions different from those in the initial disclosures, new disclosures for that service are required.

Shared systems and service providers: In a shared system, an institution need only make disclosures within its knowledge that apply to its relationship with the consumer for whom it holds an account (12 CFR 1005.4(d)). A person that provides EFT services but does not hold the consumer's account — where it issues an access device and has no agreement with the account-holding institution — must give the § 1005.7 disclosures within the purview of its relationship with the consumer (12 CFR 1005.14).

Periodic Statement Requirements Under Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.9)

General content: Periodic statements must include the same type of information required under 12 CFR 1005.9(b). The full enumeration of required line items is not reproduced in the supplied evidence and cannot be comprehensively stated here.

Exceptions to the periodic statement requirement (12 CFR 1005.9(c)):
- Passbook accounts: Where a consumer's passbook may not be accessed by an EFT other than preauthorized transfers to the account, no periodic statement need be sent, provided the institution updates the passbook (listing the amount and date of each EFT since last presented) or provides the required information on a separate document at the consumer's request (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(1)(i)).
- Preauthorized-transfer-only accounts: For other (non-passbook) accounts accessed only by preauthorized transfers to the account, the institution must send a periodic statement at least quarterly (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(1)(ii)).
- Transfers between accounts: A transfer between two accounts of the same consumer at the same institution need be documented for only one of the two accounts (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(2)). A preauthorized transfer between two such accounts is subject to the 1005.9(c)(1) preauthorized-transfer rule rather than the 1005.9(c)(2) intra-institutional rule (12 CFR 1005.9(c)(3)).
- Foreign-initiated transfers: If an EFT is initiated outside the United States, the institution need not provide a receipt or periodic statement reflecting the transfer if it treats an inquiry for clarification or documentation as a notice of error (12 CFR 1005.9(d)).

Alternative to periodic statements for payroll card accounts (12 CFR 1005.18(b)): An institution may, instead of periodic statements, make available: the account balance through a readily available telephone line; an electronic history of transactions covering at least 60 days preceding the date the consumer electronically accesses the account; and a written history provided promptly upon oral or written request covering at least 60 days preceding the date of the request (12 CFR 1005.18(b)(1)). This history must include the same type of information required on periodic statements under 1005.9(b) (12 CFR 1005.18(b)(2)).

If using this alternative, the institution must modify its initial disclosures under 12 CFR 1005.7(b) to include a telephone number to obtain the account balance, the means to obtain an electronic account history (e.g., a website address), and a summary of the consumer's right to receive a written account history upon request including a telephone number to call, plus modified error-resolution notices and annual notices as specified in 12 CFR 1005.18(c).

## Billing Errors on Open-End Credit Accounts (12 CFR 1026.13)

### What Constitutes a Billing Error [1026.13(a)]
A billing error is any of the following reflected on or with a periodic statement:
1. An extension of credit not made to the consumer or a person with actual, implied, or apparent authority to use the account.
2. An extension of credit not identified in accordance with §§ 1026.7(a)(2)/(b)(2) and 1026.8.
3. A charge for property/services not accepted by the consumer (or designee) or not delivered as agreed.
4. The creditor's failure to credit a payment or other credit properly.
5. A computational or similar accounting error made by the creditor.
6. An extension of credit for which the consumer requests additional clarification, including documentary evidence.
7. The creditor's failure to mail/deliver a periodic statement to the consumer's last known address, if that address was received in writing at least 20 days before the end of the billing cycle.

### What Makes a Billing-Error Notice 'Proper' [1026.13(b)]
A billing-error notice must be a written notice that: (1) is received at the disclosed address no later than 60 days after the creditor transmitted the first periodic statement reflecting the alleged error; (2) enables the creditor to identify the consumer's name and account number; and (3) to the extent possible, states the consumer's belief, the reasons for it, and the type, date, and amount of the error.

### Creditor's Obligations After Receiving a Proper Notice
Time limits [1026.13(c)]: The creditor must mail/deliver written acknowledgment within 30 days of receipt (unless it resolves the matter within that period), and must comply with the resolution procedures of paragraphs (e) or (f) within two complete billing cycles, but no later than 90 days, after receiving the notice.

Rules pending resolution [1026.13(d)]:
- The consumer need not pay, and the creditor may not try to collect, the disputed amount (including related finance/other charges). For automatic payment plans, the issuer must not deduct the disputed amount if the notice is received up to 3 business days before the scheduled payment date.
- No adverse credit reports (directly or indirectly) based on nonpayment of the disputed amount.
- No acceleration of the indebtedness or restricting/closing the account solely because the consumer exercised these rights in good faith; noncompliance may trigger the forfeiture penalty under 15 U.S.C. 1666(e).
- Permitted: collecting any undisputed portion, deducting the disputed amount from the credit limit, and reflecting the disputed amount on the statement if it indicates payment is not required pending compliance.

If the billing error occurred as asserted [1026.13(e)]: Within the (c)(2) time limits, correct the error, credit the account with the disputed amount and related finance/other charges, and mail/deliver a correction notice.

If no error, or a different error, occurred [1026.13(f)]: Within the (c)(2) time limits, mail/deliver an explanation of the reasons the alleged error is incorrect in whole or part; furnish copies of documentary evidence of indebtedness if requested; and if a different error occurred, correct it and credit the account accordingly.

After resolution, if the consumer still owes [1026.13(g)]: Promptly notify the consumer in writing of the amount still owed and when payment is due; allow any disclosed grace period for payment without additional charges; the creditor may report the amount as delinquent only after allowing the disclosed period or 10 days (whichever is longer); and if the consumer re-disputes in writing within the allowed period, the creditor may not report delinquency unless it also promptly reports the dispute, notifies the consumer of recipients of the report, and reports any subsequent resolution.

Reassertion [1026.13(h)]: A creditor that has fully complied has no further responsibilities (other than under (g)(4)) if the consumer reasserts substantially the same error.

Relation to Regulation E [1026.13(i)]: If the credit extension is incident to an electronic fund transfer (e.g., overdraft credit or certain hybrid prepaid-credit card transactions), the creditor must follow Regulation E error-resolution procedures (12 CFR 1005.11, 1005.18(e)) instead of paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (e), (f), and (h).

corrected_answer: Before the first transaction is made under an open-end credit plan, the creditor must furnish the account-opening disclosures required by § 1026.6 (§ 1026.5(b)(1)(i)). For open-end (not home-secured) plans, the required account-opening disclosures include, to the extent applicable (§ 1026.6(b)(2)): (1) the applicable APR(s), including each periodic rate used to compute finance charges, any introductory rate, and any rate applying after expiration of a premium initial rate (and, where permitted, a range of APRs varying by state or creditworthiness with a reference to where the applicable rate is disclosed); (2) fees for issuance or availability — any annual or other periodic fee (including activity/inactivity fees) with frequency and annualized amount, and any one-time non-periodic fee relating to opening the plan; (3) any fixed finance charge and minimum interest charge (if it exceeds the indexed $1.00 threshold); (4) transaction charges for purchases; (5) the grace period, or a statement that none is provided; (6) where required fees and/or security deposits equal 15% or more of the minimum credit limit, the available credit remaining after those amounts are debited (threshold determined on the minimum credit limit; disclosure based on the actual initial credit limit), together with a statement of the consumer's right to reject the plan and not be obligated to pay those fees until using the account or making a payment after receiving a periodic statement (§ 1026.6(b)(2)(xiii)); (7) a billing error rights reference and the Bureau website reference (§ 1026.6(b)(2)(xiv)-(xv)). Format rules (§ 1026.6(b)(1)(ii)) require specified items to appear in a table, with certain items placed directly below the table and paragraph (b)(3)-(5) disclosures permitted outside the table. Fee collection: a creditor generally may not collect any fee before account-opening disclosures are provided, though membership/application fees may be collected or agreed to beforehand if the consumer may reject the plan after receiving disclosures without obligation (§ 1026.5(b)(1)(iv)). Timing exceptions: charges not required under § 1026.6(b)(2) may be disclosed after account opening but before the consumer agrees/becomes obligated to pay, if disclosed in a manner the consumer would likely notice; and for qualifying telephone purchases, disclosures may be provided as soon as reasonably practicable after the first transaction subject to the stated return/rejection conditions (§ 1026.5(b)(1)(ii)-(iii)). For open-end high-cost mortgages, the creditor must additionally furnish the § 1026.32 disclosures at least three business days prior to account opening, including the prescribed notice, the APR, and the minimum periodic payment example (§ 1026.31(c)(1); § 1026.32(c)).

corrected_answer: Under 12 CFR 1022.43, after receiving a direct dispute notice from a consumer (submitted to a proper address under (c) and containing the required contents under (d)), a furnisher must: (1) conduct a reasonable investigation of the disputed information; (2) review all relevant information provided by the consumer with the dispute notice; (3) complete its investigation and REPORT THE RESULTS TO THE CONSUMER before expiration of the period under FCRA section 611(a)(1) (15 U.S.C. 1681i(a)(1)) within which a consumer reporting agency would be required to complete its action; and (4) if the investigation finds the furnished information was inaccurate, promptly notify each consumer reporting agency to which it provided the inaccurate information and provide any correction necessary to make the information accurate (1022.43(e)). The investigation duty applies when the dispute relates to the consumer's liability for a credit account/debt, the terms of such an account, the consumer's performance/conduct on the account, or any other information bearing on creditworthiness, credit standing, capacity, character, reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living (1022.43(a)). The duty does NOT apply where the dispute relates to identifying information (other than liability), past/present employers, inquiries, information from public records (unless furnished by a furnisher with a relationship to the consumer), fraud/active-duty alerts, or information provided by another furnisher; nor where the furnisher reasonably believes the dispute was submitted by, prepared on behalf of the consumer by, or on a form supplied by a credit repair organization (1022.43(b)). A furnisher is required to investigate only if the dispute is submitted to a proper address under 1022.43(c). The dispute notice must include: (i) sufficient identifying information (e.g., account number and consumer's name, address, telephone number); (ii) the specific information disputed and basis for the dispute; and (iii) all supporting documentation reasonably required to substantiate the dispute (1022.43(d)). A furnisher need not investigate a dispute it reasonably determines is frivolous or irrelevant — i.e., the consumer did not provide sufficient information, the dispute is substantially the same as one already addressed (unless it includes new (d) information not previously provided), or a (b) exception applies. If it so determines, the furnisher must notify the consumer of the determination within five business days by mail (or other authorized means), and the notice must state the reasons and identify any information required to investigate the dispute, which may be a standardized form (1022.43(f)).

Direct Dispute Exclusions and Frivolous/Irrelevant Dispute Handling

1. Disputes Excluded from Furnisher Investigation Requirements (12 CFR 1022.43(b)):

A. Subject-matter exclusions (1022.43(b)(1)) — the investigation requirement does not apply if the direct dispute relates to:
 (i) the consumer's identifying information (name(s), date of birth, SSN, telephone number(s), or address(es)) — other than a dispute relating to liability for a credit account/debt under (a)(1);
 (ii) the identity of past or present employers;
 (iii) inquiries or requests for a consumer report;
 (iv) information derived from public records (judgments, bankruptcies, liens, other legal matters), unless provided by a furnisher with an account/relationship with the consumer;
 (v) information related to fraud alerts or active-duty alerts; or
 (vi) information provided to a consumer reporting agency by another furnisher.
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0001][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0636_chunk_0001]

B. Credit repair organization exception (1022.43(b)(2)) — requirements do not apply if the furnisher has a reasonable belief that the dispute is submitted by, prepared on behalf of the consumer by, or submitted on a form supplied by, a credit repair organization (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 1679a(3)).
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0002][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0637_chunk_0001]

2. Frivolous or Irrelevant Disputes (12 CFR 1022.43(f)):

A furnisher is not required to investigate a direct dispute it has reasonably determined to be frivolous or irrelevant. A dispute qualifies if:
 (i) the consumer did not provide sufficient information to investigate the disputed information as required by paragraph (d);
 (ii) the dispute is substantially the same as a dispute previously submitted by or on behalf of the consumer (directly or through a CRA) for which the furnisher already satisfied applicable requirements — unless the new dispute includes paragraph (d) information not previously provided; or
 (iii) the furnisher is not required to investigate because one or more exceptions in paragraph (b) applies.
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0003][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0638_chunk_0001]

3. Consequence of a Frivolous/Irrelevant Determination (1022.43(f)(2)-(3)):

Upon making such a determination, the furnisher must notify the consumer of the determination no later than five business days after making it, by mail (or by other authorized means). The notice must state the reasons for the determination and identify any information required to investigate the disputed information, and may consist of a standardized form describing the general nature of such information.
 [12CFR1022_1022.43_chunk_0003][exam_manual_v2_2012_page_0638_chunk_0001]

Supervisory note: CFPB examiners have found that even where investigations are conducted, furnishers must actually review underlying account information, documentation, account history notes, and dispute-related correspondence; inadequate staffing and high daily dispute-resolution requirements have contributed to failures to conduct reasonable investigations.

Restrictions on the frequency and timing of debt-collector telephone calls (12 CFR 1006.14; timing under 12 CFR 1006.6):

Timing:
- A debt collector must not communicate or attempt to communicate with a consumer at any unusual time, or a time it knows or should know is inconvenient. In the absence of knowledge to the contrary, a time before 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m. local time at the consumer's location is inconvenient. The debt collector also must not contact the consumer at an unusual or inconvenient place (§ 1006.6(b)(1)).

Frequency (§ 1006.14(b)):
- General prohibition: A debt collector must not place calls or engage any person in telephone conversation repeatedly or continuously with intent to annoy, abuse, or harass any person at the called number (§ 1006.14(b)(1)).
- Presumption of compliance: A debt collector is presumed to comply if, as to a particular person and particular debt, it places calls neither (A) more than seven times within seven consecutive days, nor (B) within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with the person about that debt (the conversation date is day one) (§ 1006.14(b)(2)(i)).
- Presumption of violation: A debt collector is presumed to violate (b)(1) if it places calls in excess of either of those frequencies (§ 1006.14(b)(2)(ii)).
- Excluded calls (do not count toward the frequencies): calls placed with the person's prior direct consent within seven days of that consent; calls not connected to the dialed number; and calls to persons described in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)-(vi) (§ 1006.14(b)(3)).
- 'Particular debt' means each debt in collection; for student loans it means all student loan debts serviced under a single account number when obtained by the collector (§ 1006.14(b)(4)).

Related harassment prohibitions tied to calls include not using/threatening violence or criminal means, not using obscene or profane language, not publishing debtor lists (except as permitted), and not placing calls without meaningfully disclosing the caller's identity (§ 1006.14(c)-(g)).

Under 12 CFR 1006.6 (Regulation F / FDCPA), a debt collector's communications with a consumer are governed as follows:

1. Definition of 'consumer' (1006.6(a)): Includes the consumer, the consumer's spouse, the consumer's parent (if the consumer is a minor), legal guardian, the executor or administrator of a deceased consumer's estate, and a confirmed successor in interest.

2. Prohibited times (1006.6(b)(1)(i)): No communication at any unusual time, or a time the collector knows or should know is inconvenient. Absent knowledge to the contrary, before 8:00 a.m. and after 9:00 p.m. local time at the consumer's location is deemed inconvenient.

3. Prohibited places (1006.6(b)(1)(ii)): No communication at any unusual place, or a place the collector knows or should know is inconvenient to the consumer.

4. Place of employment (1006.6(b)(3)): No communication at the consumer's place of employment if the collector knows or has reason to know the employer prohibits the consumer from receiving such communication.

5. Attorney representation (1006.6(b)(2)): No communication with the consumer if the collector knows the consumer is represented by an attorney regarding the debt and knows, or can readily ascertain, the attorney's name and address, unless the attorney fails to respond within a reasonable time or consents to direct communication.

6. Exceptions to (b)(1)-(3) (1006.6(b)(4)): These prohibitions do not apply where the collector has the prior consent of the consumer given directly during a non-violating communication, or the express permission of a court of competent jurisdiction.

7. Cease communication (1006.6(c)): If the consumer notifies the collector in writing that they refuse to pay or want communication to cease, the collector must stop further communication about that debt, except to advise that efforts are being terminated; to notify that the collector or creditor may invoke remedies it ordinarily invokes; or, where applicable, that it intends to invoke a specified remedy.

8. Third parties (1006.6(d)): The collector generally must not communicate with persons other than the consumer, the consumer's attorney, a consumer reporting agency (if permitted by law), the creditor, the creditor's attorney, or the collector's attorney, subject to exceptions (e.g., acquiring location information under 1006.10, prior consent, court permission, or as reasonably necessary to effectuate a postjudgment judicial remedy).

## Rules Governing Payment of Interest on Interest-Bearing Deposit Accounts (12 CFR 1030.7, Regulation DD / TISA)

1. Balance Calculation (1030.7(a)(1)): Institutions must calculate interest on the full amount of principal in the account each day using either the daily balance method or the average daily balance method.

2. Minimum Balance (1030.7(a)(2)): If a minimum balance is required to earn interest, the institution must use the same method to determine the required minimum balance as it uses to calculate interest. An additional method may be used only if unequivocally beneficial to the consumer. The institution may decline to pay interest for days the balance drops below the minimum, but must pay interest on the full qualifying balance (e.g., $500 deposited against a $300 minimum earns interest on the full $500). Any computation method may be used for minimum balances not involving interest payment (e.g., fee assessment).

3. Accrual Start (1030.7(c)): Interest must begin to accrue no later than the business day on which the institution receives provisional credit for the funds, consistent with Section 606 of the Expedited Funds Availability Act and Regulation CC Section 229.14.

4. Accrual End (1030.7(c)): Interest accrues until the day funds are withdrawn.

5. Compounding/Crediting (1030.7(b)): No particular frequency is required; if the institution compounds or credits interest, it may do so annually, semi-annually, quarterly, monthly, daily, continuously, or on any other basis.

6. Early Closure (Staff Commentary 1030.7(b)-3): An institution may decline to pay accrued interest when a consumer closes an account before accrued interest is credited, provided it disclosed this practice in the initial account disclosures.

7. Definition of Interest (1030.2(n)): Interest is any payment to a consumer or account for the use of funds, calculated by applying a periodic rate to the balance. It does not include payment of a bonus or other consideration worth $10 or less during a year, the waiver or reduction of a fee, or the absorption of expenses.

8. Coverage (1030.1): Regulation DD applies to all depository institutions except credit unions that offer deposit accounts to residents of any state (including U.S. branches of foreign institutions offering accounts to consumers).

Requirements for Calculating Interest on Deposit Accounts (12 CFR 1030.7)

Permissible balance methods (1030.7(a)(1)): An institution must calculate interest on the full amount of principal in the account each day using either (1) the daily balance method — applying the daily periodic rate to the full principal each day; or (2) the average daily balance method — applying a periodic rate to the average daily balance (sum of full principal each day divided by the number of days in the period).

Prohibited methods: The ending-balance method, the low-balance method, and the investable-balance method are prohibited.

Day-count/rate rules: Institutions may apply a daily periodic rate greater than 1/365 of the interest rate (e.g., 1/360) so long as it is applied 365 days per year (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-2). In a leap year, institutions may apply a daily rate of 1/366 or 1/365 of the interest rate for 366 days if the account earns interest for February 29 (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-4).

Time accounts and dormant accounts: Institutions are not required to pay interest after a time account matures (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-5). Institutions must pay interest on funds even if the account could be treated as inactive or dormant (Staff Commentary 1030.7(a)(1)-6).

Minimum balance consistency (1030.7(a)(2)): For accounts requiring a minimum balance to earn interest, the institution must use the same method to determine the minimum balance as it uses to determine the balance on which interest is calculated; it may use an additional method only if unequivocally beneficial to the consumer.

Compounding/crediting and early closure (1030.7(b)): An institution is not required to compound or credit interest at any particular frequency; if it does, it may do so annually, semi-annually, quarterly, monthly, daily, continuously, or on any other basis. If it chooses not to pay accrued interest when a consumer closes the account before interest is credited, it must disclose this in the initial account disclosures (Staff Commentary 1030.7(b)-3).

Accrual timing (1030.7(c)): Interest must begin to accrue no later than the business day on which the institution receives provisional credit for the funds (consistent with Section 606 of the Expedited Funds Availability Act and Regulation CC Section 229.14), and interest accrues until the day funds are withdrawn.

(Related disclosure of the interest rate and APY under 1030.4(b)(1) and compounding/crediting frequency under 1030.4(b)(2) supplement these calculation requirements.)
